q: Lecture 14 – Glaucoma – slide 6: what does this picture show? Describe it.
a:
Open angle glaucoma

  • Signs
  • ocular fundus
  • initially normal
  • “cupping” of the optic disk
  • excavation (bucket) due to death of some optic nerve fibers;
  • nasal shifting of central vessels

q: Lecture 14 – Glaucoma – slide 7: what does this picture show? Describe it.
a:
Open angle glaucoma

  • Signs
  • visual field defects (after a long raised IOP)
  • enlargement of the blind spot,
  • paracentral scotoma that merges the blind spot forming an arciform scotoma

q: Lecture 14 – Glaucoma – slide 8: what does this picture show? Describe it.
a:
Open angle glaucoma

  • Signs
  • visual field defects (after a long raised IOP
  • annular ring scotoma around the fixation point (Bjerrum scotoma)
  • shrinkage and eventually loss of the nasal/temporal part of the visual field

q: Lecture 14 – Glaucoma – slide 12: what does this picture show? Describe it.
a:
Open angle glaucoma

  • Treatment
  • Argon laser trabeculoplasty:
  • Laser burns in the trabecular meshwork cause tissue contraction that widens the intervening spaces and improves outflowthrough the trabecular meshwork.
  • 50 to 100 focal laser burns placed in the anterior trabecular meshwork

q: Lecture 14 – Glaucoma – slide 14: what does this picture show? Describe it.
a:
Open angle glaucoma

  • Treatment
  • Trabeculetcomy.
  • The aqueous humor is drained through the anterior chamber through a subconjunctival scleral opening, circumventing the trabecular meshwork.
  • Formation of a thin-walled filtration bleb is a sign of sufficient drainage of aqueous humor.
  • reduction in IOP in 80–85% of cases
  • the patient must be monitored and followed for the whole life.

q: Lecture 14 – Glaucoma – slide 18: what does this picture show? Describe it.
a:
Acute primary angle closure glaucoma

  • Signs
  • edema of the upper lid,
  • tearing, conjunctival chemosis
  • epithelial edema of the cornea
  • flattening the anterior chamber associated with oval mydriasis
  • iris is congested with effacement of the iris crypt structure

q: Lecture 14 – Glaucoma – slide 20: what does this picture show? Describe it.
a:
Acute primary angle closure glaucoma

  • Signs
  • gonioscopiy iridocorneal angle is closed by iris root

q: Lecture 14 – Glaucoma – slide 23: what does this picture show? Describe it.
a:
Treatment

  • Trabeculectomy
  • Laser iridotomy
  • the fellow eye,
  • prophylactically, peripheral iridectomy
  • the patient must be monitored thoroughly for the whole life

q: Lecture 14 – Glaucoma – slide 34: what does this picture show? Describe it.
a:
Clinical forms

  • Ocular fundus
  • occlusion of the central retinal vein, diabetic retinopathy
  • neovascularization of the angle
  • vasculo endothelial growth factor originating within ischemic retina that stimulates angiogenesis

q: Lecture 14 – Glaucoma – slide 36: what does this picture show? Describe it.
a:
Congenital glaucomas

  • Symptoms and signs
  • tearing and photophobia
  • large globe dimensions
  • under three years of age the corneoscleral coat is very elastic causing the eyeball to enlarge following increased IOP
  • cornea is enlarged in all directions
  • opacities within its parenchyma
  • spontaneous tears of Descemet’s membrane
  • sclera is thin

q: Lecture 14 – Glaucoma – slide 39: what does this picture show? Describe it.
a:
Congenital glaucomas

  • Treatment
  • surgical
  • as soon as possible
  • immediately after diagnosing
  • Trabeculotomy
  • goniotomy
  • removal of this abnormal tissue within the angle
  • allowing the access of the aqueous to the outflow channels that mostly are normally developed.
